summary: This proposed standard defines a YANG extension for defining metadata annotations in YANG modules. It also specifies XML and JSON encodings for these annotations and the rules for annotating instances of YANG data nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: Network management sometimes needs extra information attached to one piece of configuration data, such as when it was last changed. This document gives a standard way to define such an extra note and to attach it to the data, in XML or in JSON.

questions: how are annotations encoded in json for yang
how do yang annotations work in xml
subtitle: A standard way to define and attach extra notes, such as a last-modified time, to YANG data, in both XML and JSON.

tldr.problem: Network management often needs to attach extra information to individual pieces of YANG-modeled data, but ad hoc annotations risk collisions, poor documentation and broken clients.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7952 defines the md:annotation YANG extension for declaring annotations in a module, and specifies how they are written as XML attributes and as JSON members.
tldr.outcome: Annotations get a module name, a namespace, a declared type and documentation, so clients can discover them and tools can understand them. The document updates RFC 6110.

today: RFC 7952 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6110 to cover the DSDL mapping of annotations.

sections.title: Why YANG Needs Metadata
sections.content:
There is a need to annotate instances of YANG (RFC 7950) data nodes with metadata. The use cases the RFC lists are: complementing regular data model information with instance-specific metadata and comments, providing information about the rendering of data in user interfaces, deactivating a subtree in a configuration datastore while keeping the data in place, and the use of metadata annotations by network management protocols in both operation requests and responses. For example, the edit-config operation in the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF), in Section 7.2 of RFC 6241, uses annotations in the form of XML attributes for identifying the location in a configuration datastore and the type of the operation.

However, metadata annotations could lead to interoperability problems if they are used in an ad hoc fashion by different parties, or without proper documentation. A sound metadata framework for YANG should therefore satisfy four requirements. The set of annotations must be extensible in a decentralized manner, so that new annotations can be defined without the risk of collisions with annotations defined and used by others. The syntax and semantics of annotations must be documented, and the documentation must be easily accessible. Clients of network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF must be able to discover all annotations supported by a given server and identify each of them correctly. And annotations sent by a server should not break clients that do not support them.

This document proposes a systematic way to define metadata annotations. The YANG extension 'annotation' is defined in the module 'ietf-yang-metadata', and other YANG modules importing that module can use the 'annotation' statement for defining one or more annotations.
sections.plainLanguage: Network management sometimes needs extra information attached to one piece of configuration data, such as when it was last changed. This document gives a standard way to define such an extra note and to attach it to the data, in XML or in JSON.

sections.title: Three New Terms
sections.content:
The document defines three terms of its own. An annotation is a single item of metadata that is attached to YANG data node instances. Metadata is additional information that complements a data tree. A metadata object is an object in JSON encoding that contains all the annotations attached to a given data node instance.

The rest of the vocabulary is borrowed. Capability, client, datastore, message, protocol operation and server come from RFC 6241. Action, anydata, anyxml, built-in type, container, data model, data node, data tree, derived type, extension, leaf, leaf-list, list and module come from RFC 7950. Attribute, document and element come from the XML Information Set, and local name, namespace name, prefix and qualified name come from XML Namespaces. Array, member, object and primitive type come from RFC 7159.
sections.plainLanguage: An annotation is one extra note. Metadata is all the extra notes together. A metadata object is where those notes live in a JSON document.

sections.title: Defining an Annotation
sections.content:
Metadata annotations are defined by the YANG extension 'md:annotation', which is defined in the module 'ietf-yang-metadata'. Its substatements are all core YANG statements: description, if-feature, reference, status, type and units.

An annotation carries a single value. The 'type' substatement, which MUST be present, takes the name of an existing built-in or derived type, and the value of the annotation MUST match that type. An annotation can be made conditional by using one or more 'if-feature' statements, and the annotation is then supported only by servers that advertise the corresponding feature. The semantics and usage rules for an annotation SHOULD be fully specified in the description, reference and units statements. The 'status' statement can be used exactly as it is used for YANG data nodes.

An annotation MUST NOT change the data tree semantics defined by YANG. Defining an annotation that allows for overriding the uniqueness of leaf-list entries, for example, is illegal. A YANG module containing one or more 'md:annotation' statements SHOULD NOT be used for defining data nodes or groupings, and derived types, identities and features SHOULD NOT be defined in such a module unless they are used by the definitions of annotations in that module.

The example in the RFC defines a 'last-modified' annotation whose type is the date-and-time type from the ietf-yang-types module, with a description saying that the annotation holds the date and time when the annotated instance was last modified or created.
sections.plainLanguage: An annotation is declared in a YANG module with a type, so its value always has a known shape. It cannot change what the data means, and it can be made conditional on a feature the server advertises.

sections.title: Using Annotations
sections.content:
By advertising a YANG module in which a metadata annotation is defined using the 'md:annotation' statement, a server indicates that it is prepared to handle that annotation according to the annotation's definition. An annotation advertised by the server may then be attached to an instance of a data node defined in any YANG module that is implemented by the server. Depending on its semantics, an annotation may have an effect only in certain data trees, or only on instances of specific types of data nodes.

A client MUST NOT add a specific annotation to data node instances if the server did not advertise it. Due care has to be exercised when introducing annotations in network management systems, in order to avoid interoperability problems and software failures caused by a client that does not understand the annotations' semantics. Generally, it is safe for a server to use annotations when the annotation is an integral part of a built-in or negotiated protocol capability, when it contains auxiliary information that is not critical for protocol operation, or when the client explicitly asks the server for it, for example through a parameter of a protocol operation request.
sections.plainLanguage: A server shows it supports an annotation by advertising the module that defines it. A client must not add an annotation the server did not advertise, and servers should use them only for information the client can safely ignore.

sections.title: Encoding Annotations in XML and JSON
sections.content:
XML attributes are a natural choice for encoding metadata in XML instance documents. For JSON (RFC 7159) there is no generally established method for encoding metadata, so the document introduces a special encoding method that is consistent with the JSON encoding of YANG data node instances defined in RFC 7951. The encoding of YANG data node instances does not change, and the namespaces of metadata annotations are encoded in the same way as the namespaces of YANG data node instances.

In XML, the local name of the attribute SHALL be the same as the name of the annotation specified in the argument of the corresponding 'md:annotation' statement. The namespace of the attribute SHALL be identified by the URI that appears as the argument of the 'namespace' statement in the YANG module where the annotation is defined, and it is RECOMMENDED that the prefix from the 'prefix' statement in that module be used in the qualified name of the attribute. The attribute value SHALL be encoded in the same way as the value of a YANG leaf instance having the same type.

In JSON, all metadata annotations assigned to a data node instance are encoded as members of a single JSON object, the metadata object. The name of an annotation member has the form 'identifier ":" identifier', where the left identifier is the name of the YANG module in which the annotation is defined and the identifier on the right is the name of the annotation. Unlike member names of data node instances, the explicit namespace identifier must always be present for annotations. The value of an annotation is encoded in exactly the same way as the value of a YANG leaf node having the same type.

The placement of the metadata object depends on the kind of data node. For a container, list entry or anydata node, the metadata object is added as a new member of that object with the name '@'. For an anyxml or leaf instance, the metadata object is added as a sibling name/value pair whose name is the symbol '@' concatenated with the name of the leaf or anyxml member being annotated. For a leaf-list entry, the annotations are added as a sibling name/array pair whose name is the symbol '@' concatenated with the name of the leaf-list, and whose value is a JSON array whose i-th element is the metadata object with annotations assigned to the i-th entry, or null if that entry has no annotations. Trailing null values in that array may be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: In XML an annotation is an extra attribute on the element. In JSON the annotations are gathered into one object, and where that object goes depends on whether the data is a container, a leaf, or a list of leaves. The module name is always written before the annotation name, with a colon.

sections.title: Representing Annotations in DSDL Schemas
sections.content:
RFC 6110 defines the standard mapping of YANG data models to Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL). This section specifies the mapping for the 'md:annotation' extension, which enables validation of XML instance documents containing metadata annotations.

The first step of the mapping procedure, the transformation of the YANG data model to the hybrid schema, is modified as follows. If the data model contains at least one 'md:annotation' statement, then a RELAX NG named pattern definition MUST be added as a child of the root grammar element in the hybrid schema, and the name '__yang_metadata__' is RECOMMENDED for it. A reference to that named pattern MUST be included as a child of every element pattern that corresponds to an anydata, container, leaf, leaf-list, or list data node. Every metadata annotation definition is mapped to an optional attribute pattern named with the prefix bound to the namespace URI of the YANG module that contains the 'md:annotation' statement, and the substatements of 'md:annotation' are mapped as described in Section 10 of RFC 6110.

The second step of the procedure, the transformation of the hybrid schema to RELAX NG, Schematron, and DSRL schemas, is unaffected by the inclusion of 'md:annotation'. The document notes that a reference is not necessary for element patterns corresponding to anyxml data nodes, because they already permit any XML attributes to be attached to their instances.
sections.plainLanguage: A schema generated from a YANG model can check that annotations are well formed. The document says how to add one shared definition of the annotations and point every data element at it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers a URI in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-metadata, with the NETMOD Working Group of the IETF as registrant contact and the note that the requested URI is an XML namespace.

It also registers a YANG module in the YANG Module Names registry, with the name ietf-yang-metadata, the same namespace, the prefix md and the reference RFC 7952. The module itself contains the 'annotation' extension statement, whose argument defines the name of the annotation and which can appear only at the top level of a YANG module or submodule. An annotation defined with this extension inherits the namespace and other context from the YANG module in which it is defined, and its data type is specified in the same way as for a leaf data node using the 'type' statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Two official lists get a new entry: the XML namespace registry and the list of YANG module names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces a mechanism for defining metadata annotations in YANG modules and attaching them to instances of YANG data nodes. By itself, this mechanism represents no security threat. The security implications of a particular annotation defined using this mechanism MUST be duly considered and documented in the annotation's definition.

An annotation SHOULD be subject to the same or stricter access control rules as the data node instance to which the annotation is attached. It is RECOMMENDED that security-sensitive or privacy-sensitive data be modeled as regular YANG data nodes rather than as annotations.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism adds no risk of its own, but each annotation has to think about its own security. An annotation should be protected at least as tightly as the data it is attached to, and sensitive data is better kept as a normal data node.

items.title: Extensible
items.text: New annotations can be defined by anyone without colliding with those defined and used by others.

items.title: Documented
items.text: The syntax and semantics of each annotation must be written down and easily accessible.

items.title: Discoverable
items.text: Clients must be able to find all annotations a server supports and identify each of them correctly.

items.text: Annotations sent by a server should not break clients that do not support them.
